Content:
Let's take a look at the function [MATH: y=f(x)], plotted below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/652f1110d2ef320572d4745134278928]

Content:
The function has a discontinuity at [MATH: x=1], but can we classify it?

Content:
Notice that when we check our continuity conditions, we find that

Content:
- [MATH: f(1) = 3], so [MATH: f(1)] exists [MATH: \,{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]
- [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\to 1} f(x) = 2], so [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\to 1} f(x)] exists [MATH: \,{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]
- [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\to 1} f(x) \neq f(1)] [MATH: \,{\color{red}{\times}}]

Content:
So the first two conditions passed, yet the third failed. When this happens, we have a point discontinuity. We also call this a removable discontinuity.

Content:
In general, a function [MATH: f(x)] has a removable discontinuity at [MATH: x=c] if

Content:
- [MATH: f(c)] exists [MATH: \,{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]
- [MATH: \displaystyle\lim_{x\to c} f(x)] exists [MATH: \,{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]
- [MATH: \displaystyle\lim_{x\to c} f(x) \neq f(c)][MATH: \,{\color{red}{\times}}]

Content:
In addition, both [MATH: f(c)] and [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\to c}f(x)] should be finite.

sections.normalized_html:
The function has a discontinuity at [MATH: x=-3.] Checking our continuity conditions, we have

  • [MATH: f(-3)= 2] exists [MATH: \,\,{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]

  • [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\to -3}f(x)= -2] exists [MATH: \,\,{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]

  • [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\to -3}f(x) \neq f(3)] [MATH: \,\,{\color{red}{\times}}]

So it's the third condition that failed, which tells us that [MATH: x=-3] is a removable discontinuity. A similar argument applies for [MATH: x=3], which is also a removable discontinuity. So, the function has removable discontinuities at [MATH: x=-3, 3.]

Note that the function also has a discontinuity at [MATH: x=0,] but it is not a removable discontinuity. Checking the conditions, we find that

  • [MATH: f(0)= -2] exists [MATH: \,\,{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]

  • [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0}f(x)] does not exist [MATH: \,\,{\color{red}{\times}}]

So this time, the second condition failed, and therefore [MATH: x=0] is not a removable discontinuity.

sections.normalized_html:
Given the function [MATH: f(x),] defined by [MATH: {x + 3,|x < 0; 0,|x = 0; 3 − x,|x > 0,]

which of the following statements are true?

  1. [MATH: \lim\limits_{x\to 0^+} f(x)=\lim\limits_{x\to 0^-} f(x)]

  2. [MATH: \lim\limits_{x\to 0} f(x)=f(0)]

  3. [MATH: f(x)] has a removable discontinuity at [MATH: x=0]
sections.readable_text:
Given the function [MATH: f(x),] defined by
[MATH: {x + 3,|x < 0; 0,|x = 0; 3 − x,|x > 0,]

which of the following statements are true?

1. [MATH: \lim\limits_{x\to 0^+} f(x)=\lim\limits_{x\to 0^-} f(x)]
2. [MATH: \lim\limits_{x\to 0} f(x)=f(0)]
3. [MATH: f(x)] has a removable discontinuity at [MATH: x=0]

sections.normalized_html:
Let's check our continuity conditions:

  • [MATH: f(0)=0] exists [MATH: \,\,{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]

  • The left and right-sided limits are [MATH: lim_(x → 0^{−})f(x) = lim_(x → 0^{−})(x + 3) = 3,; lim_(x → 0^{+})f(x) = lim_(x → 0^{+})(3 − x) = 3.] Since the left and right-sided limits are equal, we conclude that statement I is true and [MATH: \displaystyle\lim\limits_{x\to 0} f(x) = 3. \,\,{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]

  • The value of the limit is [MATH: \displaystyle\lim\limits_{x\to 0} f(x) = 3,] while the value of the function is [MATH: f(0)=0.] So, statement II is false and [MATH: \displaystyle \lim\limits_{x\to 0} f(x)\neq f(0)\,\,{\color{red}{\times}}]

Since the third condition failed, the function has a removable discontinuity at [MATH: x=0,] and statement III is true.

In conclusion, only statements I and III are true.

[IMG: /graphics/8abe220313dcb5097dcb66f6b13d2190]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The function has a discontinuity at [MATH: x=-3.] Checking our continuity conditions, we have

- [MATH: f(-3)= 2] exists [MATH: \,\,{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]
- [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\to -3}f(x)= -2] exists [MATH: \,\,{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]
- [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\to -3}f(x) \neq f(3)] [MATH: \,\,{\color{red}{\times}}]

So it's the third condition that failed, which tells us that [MATH: x=-3] is a removable discontinuity. A similar argument applies for [MATH: x=3], which is also a removable discontinuity. So, the function has removable discontinuities at [MATH: x=-3, 3.]

Note that the function also has a discontinuity at [MATH: x=0,] but it is not a removable discontinuity. Checking the conditions, we find that

- [MATH: f(0)= -2] exists [MATH: \,\,{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]
- [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0}f(x)] does not exist [MATH: \,\,{\color{red}{\times}}]

So this time, the second condition failed, and therefore [MATH: x=0] is not a removable discontinuity.

Item 8 — Example: Identifying Properties Related to Point Discontinuities Given a Function Expression

Example Prompt:
Given the function [MATH: f(x),] defined by
[MATH: {x + 3,|x < 0; 0,|x = 0; 3 − x,|x > 0,]

which of the following statements are true?

1. [MATH: \lim\limits_{x\to 0^+} f(x)=\lim\limits_{x\to 0^-} f(x)]
2. [MATH: \lim\limits_{x\to 0} f(x)=f(0)]
3. [MATH: f(x)] has a removable discontinuity at [MATH: x=0]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's check our continuity conditions:

- [MATH: f(0)=0] exists [MATH: \,\,{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]
- The left and right-sided limits are
[MATH: lim_(x → 0^{−})f(x) = lim_(x → 0^{−})(x + 3) = 3,; lim_(x → 0^{+})f(x) = lim_(x → 0^{+})(3 − x) = 3.]
Since the left and right-sided limits are equal, we conclude that statement I is true and
[MATH: \displaystyle\lim\limits_{x\to 0} f(x) = 3. \,\,{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]
- The value of the limit is [MATH: \displaystyle\lim\limits_{x\to 0} f(x) = 3,] while the value of the function is [MATH: f(0)=0.] So, statement II is false and
[MATH: \displaystyle \lim\limits_{x\to 0} f(x)\neq f(0)\,\,{\color{red}{\times}}]

Since the third condition failed, the function has a removable discontinuity at [MATH: x=0,] and statement III is true.

In conclusion, only statements I and III are true.
